newsitem.title: UK: Coffee rebounds as tight supplies persist.
newsitem.headline: Coffee rebounds as tight supplies persist.

text.p: World coffee markets rebounded on Wednesday from sharp falls earlier in the week, leading analysts to forecast that this year's blistering rally due to tight supplies might not yet be over.

Coffee futures prices, boosted by shortages of arabica beans -- the premium coffee -- from Latin America had rocketed by more than 50 percent since early 1997, triggering retail price rises by leading U.S. and European brands, before beginning to come down this week.

London's futures for robusta type beans, used mainly in the manufacture of soluble or instant coffee, fell more than seven percent on Monday to $1,535 per tonne for the widely-watched May contract on heavy selling by investment funds.
But prices have rebounded to reach a high of $1,675 by Wednesday afternoon, up $108 or seven percent on the day.

The price of May coffee on the New York futures market had risen by 10 percent on Tuesday to $1.79 a lb, which paved the way for the advance in London. By early business on Wednesday, the contract traded even higher at $1.82.

New York futures rose above $2 on March 5, the first time they had topped this level since the last big crop-damaging frost in top grower Brazil in 1994, after rising from a cyclical low around $1.15 on January 2.

"The (recent) rise has been unique because the coffee price has never moved so far, or so fast, without a disaster in Brazil," leading British commodity trade house E D & F Man said in a report this week.

While arabica supply could remain tight well into the second half of 1997 as growers are well-sold in nearby market positions, coffee prices are also vulnerable to declines if roasters (processors) finish an overdue rebuilding of low inventories and consumers resist higher supermarket prices.
But despite the recent fall, "many analysts are not convinced that the party is over," German statistician F.O. Licht said in comments published late last week.
"They expect that the market will reassert itself as supplies could become extremely limited once again, possibly even tighter than they were recently," it added.

The recent rally in coffee was driven in part by expectations of a much lower 1997/98 Brazilian crop and supply disruptions in Colombia, the next largest producer after Brazil, due to a national truck drivers' strike.
The situation has been compounded by low consumer stocks.

Until recently, roasters had been operating a hand-to-mouth buying policy based on holding minimal stocks but they were forced to replenish reserves and make extra purchases, helping to propel the rally, as values soared.
Growers took advantage of the recent high prices to ship as much coffee as possible and this created severe congestion at a number of main ports.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries, which comprises Brazil and other key exporters, decided last week to release an additional 500,000 60-kg bags of arabica coffee into the market in the first half of 1997 to help satisfy roaster demand.
At a meeting in London, the grouping agreed to revoke an agreement made in January to cut arabica exports by 300,000 bags and release another 200,000 bags.
The decision came as Colombia and other Central American producers warned that prices of more than $2 were too excessive and could curtail consumer demand.
